content: Title: Observation of van der Waals shielding between polar molecules in optical tweezersAbstract: Ultracold molecules typically suffer fast two-body loss at near-universal rates, and suppressing this loss has so far required strong DC or microwave electric fields. rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Title: Observation of van der Waals shielding between polar molecules in optical tweezers Abstract: Ultracold molecules typically suffer fast two-body loss at near-universal rates, and suppressing this loss has so far required strong DC or microwave electric fields. Recently, it has been predicted that particular pairs of molecular states can instead be shielded at zero field by repulsive van der Waals (vdW) interactions arising from either rotational or hyperfine structure. Here, we report the first experimental observation of both rotational and hyperfine vdW shielding, in collisions between pairs of laser-cooled CaF molecules trapped in optical tweezers. We observe inelastic loss suppressed by more than three orders of magnitude below the universal rate, and from measurements of thermalization we place a lower bound of 10³ on the elastic-to-inelastic ratio. We also observe three-body collisions in these shielded state combinations by deterministically preparing three molecules in a single tweezer and reading out the resulting state-resolved populations. Finally, I will present ongoing work of digital evaporative cooling of molecules. Lunch will be provided at 12:00 PM in EQuad J401.

content: Title: Quantum-computing frontiers in nuclear and particle physics Abstract: How does matter evolve in the early universe or in high-energy particle collisions? What does the phase diagram of strongly interacting matter look like? How does a large nucleus respond dynamically to probes of new physics? rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Title: Quantum-computing frontiers in nuclear and particle physics Abstract: How does matter evolve in the early universe or in high-energy particle collisions? What does the phase diagram of strongly interacting matter look like? How does a large nucleus respond dynamically to probes of new physics? Large, reliable quantum computers hold the promise of addressing these questions through first-principles simulations of matter. In this talk, I will motivate a quantum-computing program in nuclear and particle physics and describe progress toward simulating systems governed by the fundamental interactions of the Standard Model or their effective descriptions. I will present current resource estimates for selected problems and showcase recent advances in implementations on quantum hardware and in theory-algorithm-experiment codesign. These advances are laying the groundwork for addressing fundamental questions in nuclear and particle physics with quantum computers. A light lunch will be served in the Bowen Atrium at 11:45am.

title: Static-Field Shielding of Bosonic Molecules: Evaporation to Degeneracy and Self
speaker: Bound Droplets - Laura Futamura, Bakr Group
content: Title: Static-Field Shielding of Bosonic Molecules: Evaporation to Degeneracy and Self-Bound DropletsAbstract: The strong, tunable dipolar interactions of ultracold molecules make them a powerful platform for quantum many-body physics, but reaching degeneracy by evaporative cooling requires suppressing inelastic collisions. rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Title: Static-Field Shielding of Bosonic Molecules: Evaporation to Degeneracy and Self-Bound Droplets Abstract: The strong, tunable dipolar interactions of ultracold molecules make them a powerful platform for quantum many-body physics, but reaching degeneracy by evaporative cooling requires suppressing inelastic collisions. Microwave collisional shielding has enabled the preparation of degenerate Fermi gases and Bose-Einstein condensates of polar molecules, whereas static electric field shielding has been limited to fermionic species, which are less prone to inelastic loss. We demonstrate static-field Förster shielding of bosonic 23^Na87^Rb molecules, suppressing two-body loss by up to four orders of magnitude. Within a bound-state-free electric-field window, three-body loss is also strongly suppressed, enabling efficient evaporation. Evaporating with an efficiency of 2.09(9), we increase the phase-space density of the gas by two orders of magnitude, reaching degeneracy with 7200(1000) molecules. We observe self-bound droplets at the end of evaporation over a wide range of field strengths, emerging from either degenerate or non-degenerate parent gases. We perform Path Integral Monte Carlo simulations, which suggest that the observed droplets are filamentary in nature, and find good agreement with the experimentally observed droplet formation temperatures. Our results establish Förster shielding as a single-field route to prepare degenerate gases and self-bound droplets of bosonic polar molecules. Lunch will be provided at 12:00 PM in EQuad J401.

title: Quantum error correction with trapped ions
speaker: Andrew Potter, Quantinuum
content: Title: Quantum error correction with trapped ionsAbstract: To unlock the full power of quantum computers, fault-tolerant computation with error-corrected logical qubits must achieve the ultralow error rates needed for large-scale applications. This talk will highlight recent experimental progress in quantum error correction (QEC) and fault-tolerant logical operations on Quantinuum’s Helios, a 98-qubit trapped-ion quantum processor. First, I will describe demonstrations of exponential error suppression with increasing code distance for quantum
rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Title: Quantum error correction with trapped ions Abstract: To unlock the full power of quantum computers, fault-tolerant computation with error-corrected logical qubits must achieve the ultralow error rates needed for large-scale applications. This talk will highlight recent experimental progress in quantum error correction (QEC) and fault-tolerant logical operations on Quantinuum’s Helios, a 98-qubit trapped-ion quantum processor. First, I will describe demonstrations of exponential error suppression with increasing code distance for quantum memory and two-qubit logic using triangular color codes. These experiments achieved record-low logical failure rates around one error per 200,000 operations. Further, logical errors falling by more than an order of magnitude at each successive increase in code size. Second, I will present experimental validation of quantum memory and fast computation using the c4-helix code — a [[20,2,6]] non-planar code with encoding rate nearly 4x higher than surface codes, which supports a large set of fast logical Clifford gates through “instantaneous” virtual qubit relabeling (code automorphisms). A light lunch will be served in the Bowen Atrium at 11:45am.

title: Atomic Precision at Wafer Scale for Electronic and Quantum Technologies
speaker: Sheldon Zheng, MIT
content: Title: Atomic Precision at Wafer Scale for Electronic and Quantum TechnologiesAbstract: Progress in solid-state electronics has been driven by increasingly precise control over electrons, atoms, and interfaces. From controlled doping to high-κ/metal-gate stacks and gate-all-around nanosheets, each generation of silicon CMOS technology has depended on engineering matter at the scale of a few atoms. rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Title: Atomic Precision at Wafer Scale for Electronic and Quantum Technologies Abstract: Progress in solid-state electronics has been driven by increasingly precise control over electrons, atoms, and interfaces. From controlled doping to high-κ/metal-gate stacks and gate-all-around nanosheets, each generation of silicon CMOS technology has depended on engineering matter at the scale of a few atoms. Superconducting quantum computing rests on a similar foundation: the nonlinearity that defines a qubit comes from a Josephson junction whose tunnel barrier is an amorphous oxide about one nanometer thick. For future computing, from energy-efficient AI hardware to scalable quantum processors, a key challenge is to extend atomic-scale control to new materials and interfaces without sacrificing wafer-scale manufacturability. In this talk, I will introduce physical principles that allow atomic precision and wafer-scale manufacturing to coexist for emerging electronic and quantum technologies. First, I will present surface-kinetics-controlled synthesis of an air-stable monolayer superconductor at the inch scale, which reaches a kinetic inductance of ~0.7 nH/sq in superconducting circuits, together with atomically thin n-type and p-type semiconductors for CMOS applications. Second, I will discuss electrostatic-force-enabled transfer and heterogenous integration of these materials onto functional electronic and superconducting circuits with clean, minimally damaged interfaces. Finally, I will show how nano-scale strain modulates the band structures in ultra-scaled 2D transistors, delivering on-currents above 1 mA/µm at 1 V with CMOS-compatible contacts. These studies, spanning material synthesis, interface formation, and device engineering, demonstrate that atomic precision can be achieved at wafer scale and open new opportunities for energy-efficient electronics and scalable quantum technologies.

rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Title: Photon-Mediated Interactions for Quantum Sensing and Simulation Abstract: Modern atomic physics enables remarkable control over the quantum states of atoms. This control underlies technologies such as precision timekeeping and navigation, and provides sensitive probes of new physics. An important frontier is to understand how to sculpt interactions between atoms so that they develop correlations and entanglement. Such collective quantum behavior can enhance the sensitivity of measurements and enable the simulation of other quantum systems. One promising approach uses photons trapped between highly reflecting mirrors. As photons bounce back and forth between the mirrors, they can mediate interactions between laser-cooled atoms held between the mirrors. In this talk, I will discuss our efforts to sculpt these photon-mediated interactions and expand the range of collective quantum phenomena that can be realized [1-7]. I will highlight how these engineered interactions can be used to simulate the dynamical phases of superconductors [8-11] and to improve the performance of matter-wave interferometers based on de Broglie waves [2-5, 12] and optical atomic clocks [13-15]. speaker: Xing Fan, Harvard University
content: Title: Quantum Precision Measurement for Fundamental Physics Abstract: We will present a new experiment to measure CP violation beyond the Standard Model using ²²⁹ThF⁺ molecular ions. rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Title: Quantum Precision Measurement for Fundamental Physics Abstract: We will present a new experiment to measure CP violation beyond the Standard Model using ²²⁹ThF⁺ molecular ions. The ²²⁹Th nucleus has an enhanced Schiff moment due to its octupole deformation and can be efficiently produced using nuclear clock technologies. By employing advanced ion manipulation techniques, this approach aims to overcome the challenges associated with the limited availability of radioactive species. We will also present ongoing work on entangling electrons in a Penning trap. Quantum gates acting on electrons could establish a new toolbox for ion- and electron-based quantum platforms and enable quantum-logic spectroscopy of an electron’s g-factor for precision measurements. A light lunch will be served in the Bowen Atrium at 11:45am.

content: Title: Many-body effects in high harmonic generation from quantum matter Abstract: Quantum materials host intertwined charge, spin, orbital, and lattice degrees of freedom, providing a rich setting for exploring light–matter interactions. rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Title: Many-body effects in high harmonic generation from quantum matter Abstract: Quantum materials host intertwined charge, spin, orbital, and lattice degrees of freedom, providing a rich setting for exploring light–matter interactions. In the strong-field regime, high harmonic generation (HHG) connects coherent electron dynamics driven by intense lightwaves to extremely nonlinear light emission. Yet how many-body interactions shape this process on sub-optical-cycle timescales remains an open question. In this talk, I will highlight our recent efforts to understand and control HHG in quantum matter. I will first demonstrate how collective magnetism emerging at millielectronvolt energies enables switching of HHG on the petahertz frequency scale in an antiferromagnet. Turning from manipulation of the harmonic yield to the structure of the emission spectrum, I will then present our discovery of non-integer HHG arising from strong electron correlations in a cuprate Mott insulator. Together, these examples illustrate how high harmonic radiation can both reveal and be tailored by emergent many-body phenomena, opening new pathways towards lightwave electronics and attosecond technologies enabled by quantum materials.
